text: A developer needs a Postgres database for a new service. Without self-service, that means filing a ticket, waiting for a platform engineer to pick it up, then waiting again while they manually run terraform apply against a module they may not have touched in months. Multiply that across every team that needs a database or a queue, and the platform team becomes a bottleneck instead of a force multiplier.

That's the exact failure Lesson 2's 'platform as a product' framing warned about -- customers waiting in a line. The fix isn't removing Terraform from the picture. It's removing the human relay sitting in the middle of every single request, so the engine that actually provisions things is still Terraform, just triggered differently.

The fix reuses the exact mechanism from Lesson 5. A developer opens a template called something like Provision a Postgres Database, fills in a short form -- environment, size tier -- and its steps run a Terraform module with those values as variables. That terraform:run step does the same plan and apply work from your Terraform course. What changed is who triggers it: a form submission, not a ticket sitting in a backlog for two days.

The obvious question is what stops someone from provisioning something nobody approved. It isn't a human reading every request -- that's just a ticket queue with a form bolted onto the front of it. The real safety lives in what the template exposes: the module itself is fixed and already vetted, and parameters like size tier are a bounded enum, not free text, so a developer literally cannot request a configuration the platform team never signed off on.

The genuinely risky cases, like a request for the prod environment, still get a gate -- but a scoped, automated policy check or one specific on-call engineer getting a single notification, not a general queue every request sits in. And the final step still registers the new database as a Resource entity, linked by dependsOn to the service that requested it, so it's findable in the catalog instead of sitting invisible in a cloud console.

Self-service doesn't mean unconstrained; it means the constraints are enforced by the module and the form instead of a person re-explaining them on every request. Next lesson turns that same trustworthy catalog data into scorecards -- visibility into tech debt and compliance across every team at once.
